content: Dr. Rubinstein was a pioneer in the cryopreservation of umbilical cord blood and placental blood cells, enabling their use for unrelated donors in the treatment of diseases such as leukemia and genetic disorders like Tay-Sachs disease and sickle cell anemia. He also played a pivotal role in establishing an international cord blood banking system and has been a leader in the field of international cord blood transplantation. Dr. Rubinstein earned his medical degree from the Universidad de Chile in 1962. He completed his residency at Dr. I. Bassett Hospital, affiliated with Columbia University, and pursued an international fellowship at the National Institutes of Health at Mount Sinai Hospital in New York. Additionally, he served as a professor at the Universidad de Chile for four years. Following the first sibling-donor cord blood transplant in 1988, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) awarded Dr. Rubinstein a grant to develop the world’s first cord blood program at the New York Blood Center. This program aimed to create an inventory of stem cell units necessary to provide unrelated, matched grafts for patients. In 1993, Dr. Joanne Kurtzberg at Duke University Medical Center performed the first two successful unrelated donor cord blood transplants, one of which cured a case of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). By 2006, over 7,000 unrelated donor transplants had been performed worldwide. Dr. Rubinstein is the co-founder and director of the National Cord Blood Program at the New York Blood Center. Alongside his wife and co-founder, Dr. Cladd Stevens, he has facilitated the growth of an inventory of umbilical cord blood units from ethnically diverse donors, ensuring that the program meets the needs of patients globally. Dr. Rubinstein specializes in immunogenetics, a field that examines the structure and function of genes regulating immune responses, influencing the acceptance or rejection of tissue and organ transplants, and determining susceptibility to certain diseases. He began his career as an investigator at the Lindsley F. Kimball Research Institute at the New York Blood Center and currently serves as the director of the Fred H. Allen Jr. Laboratory of Immunogenetics. He is also an adjunct clinical professor at Columbia University and has authored over 200 research papers on immunogenetics, cord blood banking, and transplantation.
